labour.e: From Middle English labor, labour, labur, from Old French labor (modern labeur) and its etymon, Latin labor.
labour.g: An effort expended on a particular task; toil, work.

labour.e: From Middle English labouren, from Old French laborer, from Latin laborare (“(intransitive) to labor, strive, exert oneself, suffer, be in distress, (transitive) to work out, elaborate”), from labor (“labor, toil, work, exertion”); perhaps remotely akin to robur (“strength”).

lace.e: From Middle English lace, laace, las, from Old French las, from Vulgar Latin *laceum, based on Latin laqueus.
lace.g: A light fabric containing patterns of holes, usually built up from a single thread.

lace.e: From Middle English lacen, lasen, from Old French lacer, lacier, lasser, lachier, from the noun (see above).

lack.e: From Middle English lack, lakke, lak, from Old English *læc (“deficiency, lack, want”), from Proto-West Germanic *lak, from Proto-Germanic *laką, *lakaz (“slackness”), from Proto-Germanic *lakaz (“limp, slack, loose, low”), related to *lak(k)ōną (“to blame, reproach”), from Proto-Indo-European *lok-néh₂-.
lack.g: A deficiency or need (of something desirable or necessary); an absence, want, dearth.

lack.e: From Middle English lacken, lakken, laken, from Old English læccian, *lacian (“to blame, criticise, lack”), from Proto-West Germanic *lak(k)ōn (“to blame, be lacking”), from Proto-Germanic *lak(k)ōną (“to reproach, blame, be lacking”), from Proto-Indo-European *lok-néh₂-.
lack.g: To be without, not to have, to need, to require.

lad.e: From Middle English ladde (“foot soldier, servant; male commoner; boy”), from late Old English *ladda (attested in Old English personal byname Ladda), probably of North Germanic origin.

ladder.e: From Middle English ladder, laddre; from Old English hlǣder, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaidriju, from Proto-Germanic *hlaidrijō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlóydʰrom, from *ḱley- (“to lean”). Further cognates include Ashkun istrī, Kamkata-viri c̣ik, Prasuni čik, čix; Waigali c̣iř, Sanskrit श्रिति (śrití).
ladder.g: A frame, usually portable, of wood, metal, or rope, used for ascent and descent, consisting of two side pieces to which are fastened rungs (

lade.e: From Middle English laden, from Old English hladan and Old English hleadan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaþan, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną (“to load”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂- (“to put, lay out”).
lade.g: To fill or load (related to cargo or a shipment).

lade.e: From Middle English lad, from Old English lād, from Proto-Germanic *laidō (“a way, course”).

ladies.e: As a lavatory for women, via misspelling of ladies'.
ladies.g: A ladies' room: a lavatory intended for use by women.

ladle.e: From Middle English ladel, from Old English hlædel, derived from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną (“to load”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂- (“to put, lay out”), same source as Lithuanian kloti (“to spread”), equivalent to lade + -le (“agent suffix”).
ladle.g: A deep-bowled spoonlike utensil with a long, usually curved, handle.

lady.e: From Middle English lady, laddy, lafdi, lavedi, from Old English hlǣfdīġe (“mistress of a household, wife of a lord, lady”, literally “bread-kneader”), from hlāf (“bread, loaf”) + dǣġe (“kneader”), related to Old English dǣġe (“maker of dough”) (whence dey (“dairymaid”)). Unrelated to lad.

lair.e: From Middle English leir, leire, lair, lare, from Old English leġer (“couch, bed”), from Proto-Germanic *legrą, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-.
lair.g: A place inhabited by a wild animal, often a cave or a hole in the ground.

lake.e: Middle English lake (“small stream of running water, pool, lake”), from Old English lacu (“stream, pool, pond, lake”), from Proto-West Germanic *laku, from Proto-Germanic *lakō (“stream, pool, body of water", originally "a place where water runs off and collects”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leg- (“to leak, drain”).
lake.g: A large, landlocked stretch of water or similar liquid.

lake.e: From Northern Middle English lake, lak, lac (also laik, layke; Southern loke), from Old English lāc (“play, sport, strife, battle, sacrifice, offering, gift, present, booty, message”), from Proto-West Germanic *laik, from Proto-Germanic *laikaz (“game, dance, hymn, sport”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“to bounce, shake, tremble”).

lama.g: lamé (fabric with silver or gold threads woven in)

lamb.e: From Middle English lamb, from Old English lamb, from Proto-West Germanic *lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz, probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₁l̥h₁onbʰos, enlargement of *h₁elh₁én, ultimately from *h₁el-.
lamb.g: A young sheep; especially, one younger than nine months.

lame.e: From Middle English lame, from Old English lama (“lame”), from Proto-West Germanic *lam, from Proto-Germanic *lamaz (“lame”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃lemH- (“to tire; to break”).
lame.g: Unable to walk properly because of a problem with one's feet or legs.

lame.e: From Middle French lame, from Latin lāmina.
lame.g: A thin layer or plate of material, as in certain kinds of armor.

lament.e: A back-formation from lamentation or else from Middle French lamenter and its etymon Latin lāmentor (“to wail, weep”), from lāmentum (“wailing, moaning, weeping”); with formative -mentum, from the root *la-, probably ultimately imitative.
lament.g: An expression of grief, suffering, sadness or regret.

lamentable.e: From Middle English lamentable, from Middle French lamentable, from Latin lāmentābilis (“full of sorrow, mournful; deplorable”), from lāmentor (“lament”), from lāmenta (“wailing, weeping”). By surface analysis, lament + -able.
lamentable.g: Causing sorrow, distress or regret; deplorable, pitiful or distressing.

lamentation.e: Recorded since 1375, from Middle English lamentacioun, from Middle French lamentation and its etymon Latin lāmentātiō (“wailing, moaning, weeping”), from the deponent verb lāmentor, from lāmentum (“wail; wailing”), itself from a Proto-Indo-European *leh₂- (“to howl”), presumed ultimately imitative. Replaced Old English cwiþan.

lamp.e: From Middle English laumpe, lampe, from Old French lampe (“lamp, light”), from Latin lampas (“torch, lamp, light”), from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “torch, lamp, beacon, light, meteor”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂p- (“to shine”).
lamp.g: A device that generates light, heat, or other electromagnetic radiation. Especially an electric light bulb.

lampstand.g: A menorah or other holder or stand for a lamp.

lance.e: From Middle English launce, from Old French lance, from Latin lancea.
lance.g: A weapon of war, consisting of a long shaft or handle and a steel blade or head; a spear carried by horsemen.

lancet.e: From Middle English launcet, from Old French lancete, a diminutive of lance. By surface analysis, lance + -et.
lancet.g: A sharp, pointed, two-edged surgical instrument used in venesection and for opening abscesses etc.

land.e: From Middle English lond, land, from Old English land, from Proto-West Germanic *land, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”), from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”). Non-Germanic cognates include Old Irish lann (“heath”), Welsh llan (“enclosure”), Breton lann (“heath”), Old Church Slavonic лѧдо (lędo).
land.g: The part of Earth which is not covered by oceans or other bodies of water.

land.e: From Middle English *land, from Old English hland.

landed.e: From Middle English londed, from Old English ġelandod. By surface analysis, land + -ed.

landing.g: An arrival at a surface, as of an airplane or any descending object.

landmark.e: From Middle English *landmark, from Old English landmearc (“boundary”), from Proto-West Germanic *landamarku (“boundary, landmark”). Equivalent to land + mark.
landmark.g: An object that marks the boundary of a piece of land (usually a stone, or a tree).

lane.e: From Middle English lane, lone, from Old English lanu (“a lane, alley, avenue”), from Proto-West Germanic *lanu, from Proto-Germanic *lanō (“lane, passageway”).
lane.g: A road, street, or similar thoroughfare.

language.e: From Middle English langage, language, from Old French language, from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”), from Old Latin dingua (“tongue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue, speech, language”).
language.g: A body of words, and set of methods of combining them (called a grammar), understood by a community and used as a form of communication.
A languet, a flat plate in or below the flue pipe of an organ.

languish.e: From Middle English languysshen, from the present participle stem of Anglo-Norman and Middle French languir, from Late Latin languīre, alteration of Latin languēre (“to be faint, unwell”). : Compare languor, languid and lax. : Cognate with slack.
languish.g: To lose strength and become weak; to be in a state of weakness or sickness.

lantern.e: From Middle English lanterne (13th century), via Old French lanterne from Latin lanterna (“lantern”), itself a corruption of Ancient Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptḗr, “torch”) (see lamp, λάμπω (lámpō)) by influence of Latin lucerna (“lamp”).
lantern.g: A case of translucent or transparent material made to protect a flame, or light, used to illuminate its surroundings.

lap.e: From Middle English lappe, from Old English læppa (“skirt or flap of a garment”), from Proto-West Germanic *lappō, from Proto-Germanic *lappô (“cloth; rag”), of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”).
lap.g: The loose part of a coat; the lower part of a garment that plays loosely; a skirt; an apron.

lap.e: From Middle English lappen, from Old English lapian, from Proto-West Germanic *lapōn, from Proto-Germanic *lapōną, *lapjaną (“to lick; lap”), from imitative Proto-Indo-European *leh₂b- (“to lap, lick”); akin to Old High German laffen (“to lick”), Old Norse lepja, Danish labe, Old Saxon lepil, German Löffel (“spoon”). French lamper is a loanword from German.
lap.g: To take (liquid) into the mouth with the tongue; to lick up with a quick motion of the tongue.

lapse.e: From Middle French laps, from Latin lāpsus, from lābī (“to slip”).

lapwing.e: From Middle English lapwynge, lapwynke, lappewincke, lapwynche, lhapwynche, from Old English hlēapewince (“lapwing”), from Old English hlēapan (“to leap”) + wincian (“to wink, make a sign”), due to its manner of flight. The modern form is influenced by folk etymology to resemble English wing.
lapwing.g: Any of several medium-sized wading birds belonging to the subfamily Vanellinae, within family Charadriidae.

large.e: From Middle English large, from Old French large, from Latin larga, feminine of largus (“abundant, plentiful, copious, large, much”), of uncertain ultimate origin; see there for more. Along with big, it mostly displaced Middle English stoor and muchel (the latter surviving in much under a different meaning).
large.g: Of considerable or relatively great size or extent.

lash.e: From Middle English lashe, lasshe, lasche (“a stroke; the flexible end of a whip”), from Proto-Germanic *laskô (“flap of fabric, strap”).
lash.g: The thong or braided cord of a whip, with which the blow is given.

last.e: From Middle English laste, latst, syncopated variant of latest, both ultimately from Old English latost.
last.g: Final, ultimate, coming after all others of its kind.

last.e: From Middle English lasten, from Old English lǣstan, from Proto-West Germanic *laistijan, from Proto-Germanic *laistijaną.

latch.e: From Middle English lacchen (“to seize, catch, grasp”, verb), from Old English læċċan (“to grasp, take hold of, catch, seize”), from Proto-Germanic *lakjaną, *lakwijaną, *lakkijaną (“to seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂g-, *(s)leh₂gʷ- (“to take, seize”).
latch.g: To close or lock as if with a latch.

latch.e: From Middle English latche, lacche (“a latch; a trap”), from lacchen (“to seize, catch, grasp”), from Old English læċċan (“to grasp, take hold of, catch, seize”).
latch.g: A fastening for a door that has a bar that fits into a notch or slot, and is lifted by a lever or string from either side.

latchet.e: From Middle English lachet, from Old French lachet, variant of lacet, diminutive of laz (“lace”).
latchet.g: A small lever action crossbow with the cocking lever built into the top of the stock and a top mounted trigger.
A small latch, as for a gate.

late.e: From Middle English late, lat, from Old English læt (“slow; slack, lax, negligent; late”), from Proto-West Germanic *lat, from Proto-Germanic *lataz (“slow, lazy”). By surface analysis, deverbal from let.
late.g: Near the end of a period of time.

lately.e: From Middle English lately, latly, equivalent to late + -ly.
lately.g: Recently; not long ago; of late; not long since.

later.e: From Middle English later, latere, from Old English lator, equivalent to late + -er. Adjective: From Middle English later, latere, from Old English lætra, equivalent to late + -er.

latest.e: From Middle English lateste, from Old English latost, latest, lætest, superlative of læt, whence English late.
latest.g: The most recent thing, particularly information or news.

latrine.e: From French latrine (“latrine”), from Latin lātrīna.
latrine.g: An open trench or pit used for urination and defecation.

latter.e: From Middle English latter, lattere, lattre, from Old English lætra, comparative form of læt (“late”). Equivalent to late + -er, thus a doublet of later; also, related to last, whose doublet is latest.

lattice.e: From Middle English latis, from Middle French lattis (“lathing”), from Old French lattis, from latte (“a lath”), from Frankish *lattu (“a lath”), from Proto-Germanic *laþô (“board; plank; ledge”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)latn-, *(s)lat- (“beam; log”).
lattice.g: A flat panel constructed with widely-spaced crossed thin strips of wood or other material, commonly used as a garden trellis.

laud.e: From Middle English lauden, from Old French lauder, from Latin laudō, laudāre, from laus (“praise, glory, fame, renown”), from echoic Proto-Indo-European root *leh₁wdʰ- (“song, sound”).

laugh.e: From Middle English laughen, laghen, from (Anglian) Old English hlæhhan, hlehhan, (West Saxon) hliehhan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlahhjan, from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną. Indo-European: Breton kloc'h (“bell”), Irish clog (“bell.
laugh.g: An expression of mirth particular to the human species; the sound heard in laughing; laughter.

laughing.e: From Middle English laughynge; equivalent to laugh + -ing.
laughing.g: verbal adjective of laugh: the action of the verb to laugh.

laughter.e: From Middle English laughter, laghter, laȝter, from Old English hleahtor (“laughter, jubilation, derision”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *klek-, *kleg- (“to shout”).
laughter.g: The sound of laughing, produced by air so expelled; any similar sound.

launch.e: From Middle English launchen (“to throw as a lance”), Old French lanchier, another form (Old Northern French/Norman variant, compare Jèrriais lanchi) of lancier, French lancer, from lance.
launch.g: To throw (a projectile such as a lance, dart or ball); to hurl; to propel with force.

launch.e: From Portuguese lancha (“barge, launch”), apparently from Malay lancar (“quick, agile”). Spelling influenced by the verb above.
launch.g: The boat of the largest size and/or of most importance belonging to a ship of war, and often called the "captain's boat" or "captain's launc

laurel.e: From Middle English laurer, laurel, from Anglo-Norman lorer, from Old French lorier, from Vulgar Latin *laurārius, from Latin laurus (“laurel”).
laurel.g: An evergreen shrub of species Laurus nobilis, having aromatic leaves of a lanceolate shape, with clusters of small, yellowish white flowers

laver.e: From Middle English laver, lavre, lever, levre, laber (“a kind of water plant”), from Old English læfer, leber (“a rush (plant)”), a borrowing from Latin laver (“water plant”).
laver.g: A red alga/seaweed, Porphyra umbilicalis (syn. Porphyra laciniata), eaten as a vegetable.

laver.e: From Middle English laver, lavour, from Old French laveoir, laveor, laveour, lavor, lavur, from Latin lavātōrium.
laver.g: Where one laves, a washroom, particularly a lavatorium, the washing area in a monastery.

lavish.e: From Middle English laves, lavas, lavage (“extravagant, wasteful, prodigal”), from lavas (“excessive abundance”), from Old French lavasse, lavache (“torrent of rain”); possibly later conflated in some senses by Middle English laven (“to pour out”), equivalent to lave + -ish.
lavish.g: Expending or bestowing profusely; profuse; prodigal.

law.e: From Middle English lawe, laȝe, from Old English lagu (“law”), borrowed from Old Norse lǫg (“law”, literally “things laid down or firmly established”), originally the plural of lag (“layer, stratum, a laying in order, measure, stroke”), from Proto-Germanic *lagą (“that which is laid down”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”).
law.g: The body of binding rules and regulations, customs, and standards established in a community by its legislative and judicial authorities.

law.e: From Northern Middle English lawe, from Old English hlāw (“burial mound”).

lawbreaker.e: From Middle English lawbreker, lawe brekare; equivalent to law + breaker.
lawbreaker.g: One who breaks (violates) the law, a criminal.

lawful.e: From Middle English laweful, equivalent to law + -ful, conflated with Middle English leful, leeful, leveful (“according to law, lawful, pertaining to law”).
lawful.g: Conforming to, or recognised by the laws of society.

lawfully.e: From Middle English lawefully, lawfulliche, lawefulliche; equivalent to lawful + -ly.

lawgiver.e: From Middle English lawe ȝivere, lawe-ȝivere, law ȝevar; equivalent to law + giver.
lawgiver.g: One who provides laws to a society.

lawless.e: From Middle English laweles; equivalent to law + -less.

lawsuit.g: In civil law, a case where two or more people disagree and one or more of the parties take the case to a court for resolution.

lawyer.e: From Middle English lawiere, lawier, lawer, equivalent to law + -yer.
lawyer.g: A professional person with a graduate law degree that qualifies for legal work (such as Juris Doctor)

layer.e: Appears at first glance to be from Middle English leyer, leyare (“a layer of stones or bricks”), equivalent to lay + -er. In which case, ultimately identical to etymology 2 below. For the pronunciation compare prayer.
layer.g: A single thickness of some material covering a surface.

lazy.e: Probably from Low German and Middle Low German lasich (“slack, feeble, lazy”), from las, from Old Saxon lask, from Proto-Germanic *lasiwaz, *laskaz (“feeble, weak”), from Proto-Indo-European *las- (“weak”).
lazy.g: Unwilling to do work or make an effort; disinclined to exertion.
